meta.notes: [clf batch 1: 14 scenario rewrites] [clf batch 2: 15 scenario rewrites — IGW, Snowball, Global Accelerator, Artifact, Marketplace, Region/AZ, Step Functions, Secrets Manager, Deep Archive, PrivateLink, Budgets, IAM policies, Support plans, SES, DataSync] [clf batch 3: 15 rewrites + 4 FACTUAL FIXES: aws-003 cross-region replication, aws-004 RI vs On-Demand discount, aws-013 stem/options mismatch, aws-019 CloudTrail vs CloudWatch] [clf batch 4: 15 rewrites + 1 FACTUAL FIX: aws-030 NAT GW vs VPN GW] [clf batch 5: 18 rewrites + 4 FACTUAL FIXES: aws-043/045/056/058] [clf batch 6 (final): 21 rewrites + 4 FACTUAL FIXES: aws-068/071/072/092. CLF-C02 FULLY REWRITTEN.]

questions.question: An auditor asks who is responsible for hypervisor patching, physical-data-centre security, customer's EC2 guest OS hardening, and customer's IAM-policy design. The customer answers with one model published by AWS. Which is the correct division?
options: AWS manages every layer including data, IAM, and OS — false
Customers run physical data-centre security and the global backbone — false
AWS secures the cloud (hardware, hypervisor, facilities, global network); customers secure what they put IN the cloud (data, IAM, OS, app config)
AWS handles every compliance requirement transparently — false, compliance is shared
questions.explanation: AWS is responsible for security OF the cloud (hardware, facilities, global infrastructure). Customers are responsible for security IN the cloud (data, IAM, OS patching on EC2, etc.).

questions.question: A team needs durable OBJECT storage for any size of file, REST-API-accessible, with 99.999999999% (11 nines) durability and globally addressable URLs. They don't need a POSIX filesystem. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon EBS — block storage for EC2 only, not object
Amazon S3 — object storage with 11-nines durability, HTTPS access, virtually unlimited scale
Amazon EFS — POSIX NFS file system, not the object/REST scenario described
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD, lost on stop
questions.explanation: Amazon S3 (Simple Storage Service) is AWS's object storage service. It stores data as objects in buckets, offers 99.999999999% (11 9s) durability.

questions.question: A startup wants the LOWEST latency for users in Tokyo, São Paulo, and Frankfurt. The architect proposes deploying the same application stack in AWS Regions geographically close to each user population (e.g., ap-northeast-1, sa-east-1, eu-central-1). What is the PRIMARY benefit of using these distinct Regions?
options: Lower latency to nearby users PLUS regional data-residency for local regulations — the genuine benefit of multi-Region geographic deployment
Automatic synchronous replication of all services across every Region by default — FALSE; cross-Region replication is opt-in per service and is NEVER 'default'
Identical published prices across every Region — FALSE; per-Region pricing varies
Free inter-Region data transfer for active-active workloads — FALSE; inter-Region transfer is billable
questions.explanation: Deploying into geographically closer Regions reduces latency for nearby users and supports data-residency requirements. AWS does NOT automatically replicate services across Regions; each service requires explicit configuration (S3 CRR, DynamoDB Global Tables, etc.). Per-Region pricing varies. Inter-Region traffic is billable. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked a factually false claim about default cross-Region replication) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A workload runs the SAME m5.large fleet 24×7 with no changes for the next 3 years. The finance team wants the BIGGEST possible compute discount in exchange for a multi-year commitment. Which EC2 pricing model fits?
options: On-Demand per-second — NO commitment, NO discount; the most expensive per-hour option
Spot Instances — up to ~90% off but INTERRUPTIBLE; unsuitable for steady production workloads
Reserved Instances (or Savings Plans) with 3-year all-upfront term — up to 72% discount in exchange for the multi-year commitment described
Dedicated Hosts — physical-host isolation pricing, NOT the deepest-discount steady-workload model
questions.explanation: For a STEADY, multi-year workload, the deepest discount comes from 3-year all-upfront Reserved Instances (up to 72%) or Compute Savings Plans (similar). On-Demand has NO commitment and NO discount. Spot is cheaper but interruptible. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked On-Demand as the cheapest model, which is exactly backwards) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A streaming site serves 90% static assets (videos, images) and is hit by viral traffic spikes from specific countries. Latency to those geographies dominates user-perceived performance. Which AWS service caches the assets at edge locations close to viewers and absorbs the spike load before it reaches the origin?
options: Amazon Route 53 — DNS routing, no edge caching of asset bytes
AWS Site-to-Site VPN — corporate VPN, not a CDN
Application Load Balancer — regional L7 LB at the origin, not at the edge
Amazon CloudFront — global CDN with 600+ edge POPs caching assets near viewers
questions.explanation: Amazon CloudFront is a CDN that distributes content from edge locations worldwide, reducing latency for end users by serving cached content from the nearest edge location.

questions.question: A developer needs to run a Python function in response to S3 object-creation events with NO server to provision, NO OS to patch, billing in 1 ms increments only when the function runs. Which AWS service fits?
options: AWS Lambda — serverless function-as-a-service: event-driven, no infra, per-ms billing, ≤15 min execution
Amazon EC2 — VMs that the customer must provision, patch, and pay for hourly while idle
Amazon ECS — container orchestrator that still needs the customer to manage container infra (or run on Fargate)
Amazon Lightsail — bundled small-VM offering, still customer-managed instances
questions.explanation: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service. You upload code and Lambda runs it in response to events. You pay only for execution time — no server management required.

questions.question: An EC2 instance must be granted read-only permission to a specific S3 bucket. Best practice in AWS is to attach a ROLE with the minimum permissions to the instance, not store an access key on disk. Which AWS service models who/what can do what on AWS resources via users, groups, roles, and policies?
options: AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) — users, groups, roles, and policies that authorise actions on AWS resources
AWS Internet Access Management — not a real service name
AWS Infrastructure and Application Management — not a real service name
AWS Image and AMI Management — not a real service name
questions.explanation: IAM (Identity and Access Management) controls authentication (who you are) and authorization (what you can do) in AWS through users, groups, roles, and policies.

questions.question: AWS infrastructure inside one Region is partitioned into multiple physically isolated facility groups, each with its OWN power, cooling, and network — connected to each other by sub-ms private fibre. A Region typically has 3+ of these. What's the AWS term for one of these facility groups?
options: Availability Zone (AZ) — one or more discrete data centres with redundant power and networking inside a Region
Region — the geographic AREA that CONTAINS the AZs; opposite scope
Edge Location / CloudFront POP — global edge cache, not a Region-internal facility
VPC subnet — a customer logical network primitive, not AWS physical infrastructure
questions.explanation: An AZ is one or more data centers within a Region with independent power, cooling, and networking. Multiple AZs in a Region enable high availability architecture.

questions.question: A regulated-industry customer running mission-critical workloads on AWS wants a named human on the AWS side: a Technical Account Manager who knows their architecture, reviews quarterly business reviews, and acts as their primary escalation. Which AWS Support plan includes a dedicated TAM by default?
options: Developer support — email-only support during business hours, no TAM
Enterprise support — includes a dedicated Technical Account Manager (TAM) and 15-minute critical-case response
Basic support — billing and account help only, no technical support, no TAM
Business support — 24×7 chat/phone/email and Trusted Advisor, but no dedicated TAM
questions.explanation: The Enterprise Support plan includes a dedicated TAM, concierge support, and 15-minute response time for business-critical issues. Business plan has < 1 hour response.

questions.question: The Well-Architected Framework has six pillars. ONE pillar covers the workload's ability to recover from failures, automatically scale, test recovery procedures, and meet RTO/RPO. Which pillar is this?
options: Security — protecting data + systems, but not the recover-from-failure pillar
Reliability — recovery from failure, scaling, testing recovery, RTO/RPO
Cost Optimisation — financial efficiency, not failure recovery
Performance Efficiency — using resources efficiently, not the same as reliability
questions.explanation: The Reliability pillar of the Well-Architected Framework focuses on recovery from disruptions, dynamic resource acquisition, and mitigating misconfigurations.

questions.question: A security audit asks: who made an `iam:DeleteUser` call against the production account at 14:47 UTC yesterday, from which IP, with which user-agent, and what parameters were used? The answer must come from the tenant-wide management-plane log. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudWatch — metrics + log AGGREGATION, but not the canonical control-plane audit trail
AWS CloudFormation — IaC deployment, not an audit log
AWS Transit Gateway — networking hub, unrelated to audit
AWS CloudTrail — the tenant-wide control-plane audit log: who, when, from where, what API, parameters
questions.explanation: CloudTrail records all API calls made to AWS services, providing an audit log of who did what, when, and from where. Essential for compliance and security investigations.

questions.question: An architect designs a NETWORK construct inside an AWS account that has customer-defined private IP ranges (CIDR), customer-defined subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, and security groups. The construct is LOGICALLY ISOLATED from other accounts. Which AWS resource is this?
options: An EC2 instance — a single VM, not the network construct described
The AWS Global Backbone — AWS's private inter-Region network, customer can't define CIDR on it
A Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) — customer-defined logically isolated virtual network with CIDR, subnets, route tables, NACLs, SGs
Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes, not a network construct
questions.explanation: A VPC is the canonical AWS virtual network primitive: customer-defined IP ranges, subnets per AZ, route tables, NACLs, SGs, gateways. PRIOR VERSION HAD A MISMATCH between the stem (about steady-state pricing) and the marked-correct answer (about VPC). Rewritten for consistency 2026-05-13.

questions.question: Architecture-101 distinguishes two scaling models. Adding MORE machines and distributing load across them is one; replacing the existing machine with a BIGGER one is the other. Which mapping is correct?
options: Horizontal = use bigger instances; Vertical = launch more instances — reversed
Horizontal applies only to databases; Vertical applies only to compute — false dichotomy
The terms describe the same pattern — false
Horizontal = scale OUT by adding instances; Vertical = scale UP to a larger instance
questions.explanation: Horizontal scaling (scale out/in) adds/removes instances. Vertical scaling (scale up/down) resizes the instance to a larger/smaller type. AWS Auto Scaling handles horizontal scaling.

questions.question: An architect needs to estimate the MONTHLY cost of a planned deployment (10 EC2 m6i.xlarge + 5 TB S3 Standard + 1 RDS db.m5.large + 100 GB data transfer) BEFORE provisioning anything. Which AWS tool produces a per-service estimate from the catalogue pricing?
options: AWS Cost Explorer — analyses ALREADY-incurred costs; no pre-deployment estimate
AWS Pricing Calculator — public web tool for estimating monthly cost from catalogue prices before deployment
AWS Budgets — alerts on real spend versus a threshold; doesn't estimate plans
AWS Trusted Advisor — best-practice recommendations on running infra, not pre-deploy pricing
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator lets you estimate monthly costs for AWS services before you deploy them. Cost Explorer analyzes existing costs; Budgets sets alerts.

questions.question: A web tier sized for steady traffic gets bursty afternoon spikes. The team wants the fleet to GROW to absorb peak and SHRINK when demand drops, automatically based on CPU and request-count metrics, without operator intervention. Which AWS feature?
options: EC2 instance-family swap — manual right-sizing, not dynamic capacity adjustment
Automated OS patching — operational, not capacity scaling
AWS Auto Scaling (EC2 Auto Scaling Groups + scaling policies) — automatic add/remove based on demand signals
Scheduled RDS / EBS backups — backup, not capacity
questions.explanation: AWS Auto Scaling monitors applications and automatically adjusts capacity (EC2 instances, ECS tasks, etc.) to maintain performance and minimize costs.

questions.question: A finance team is comparing cloud to traditional data-centre TCO. The AWS sales rep keeps using the phrase 'pay only for what you use'. The finance lead asks for a concrete definition in pricing terms. Which best describes this principle?
options: Consumption-based pricing — billing is per actual usage (per hour/second/GB/request), no upfront seat or hardware fee
Per-resource flat fee — charge regardless of usage, the data-centre licensing model
Flat monthly subscription — fixed monthly regardless of consumption
Upfront annual licensing — pay once for a year of access, the perpetual-software model
questions.explanation: One of the key cloud benefits: consumption-based pricing. Unlike on-premises infrastructure with fixed costs, cloud billing is based on actual consumption.

questions.question: A security investigator needs a per-API-call record: WHO (IAM principal), WHEN (timestamp), FROM WHERE (source IP / user-agent), WHAT (API name), WITH WHAT (request parameters). This is the AWS API auditing surface — distinct from metrics/logs aggregated by CloudWatch. Which AWS service provides exactly this audit trail?
options: AWS CloudTrail — records every API call across the account with caller identity, time, IP, parameters
AWS Inspector — vulnerability/host assessment, not API call audit
AWS Config — resource-configuration history, not per-API-call audit
Amazon CloudWatch — metrics + log aggregation; useful but NOT the per-API audit trail described
questions.explanation: CloudTrail is the AWS API-call audit log: every `Action` against any service is recorded with caller identity, time, source IP, user-agent, and parameters. CloudWatch is metrics + log aggregation — not the per-API audit trail. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked CloudWatch) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A security team wants to grant the IAM principal `arn:aws:iam::111:role/web` access to a specific S3 bucket and deny everyone else. The control is written as a JSON document attached to the bucket itself (not to any IAM identity). Which control type is this?
options: An S3 bucket policy — a JSON resource policy attached to the bucket; the canonical mechanism for bucket-level grants/denies
An EC2 instance profile — attaches a role to an EC2 instance; not a bucket-side control
An S3 lifecycle policy — transitions/expirations; not access control
Default bucket encryption — encrypts at rest; not access control
questions.explanation: S3 bucket policies are JSON-based resource policies that control who can access a bucket and what actions they can perform. They can grant access to other AWS accounts.

questions.question: A workload's web tier in a public subnet needs bidirectional internet connectivity. The route table for that subnet must have a default route pointing at a VPC-level component. Which component fits this role?
options: Internet Gateway — bidirectional internet ingress/egress for public-subnet resources
VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately; no internet path
Network ACL — stateless subnet firewall, not a gateway
NAT Gateway — egress-only for private subnets; not bidirectional
questions.explanation: An Internet Gateway (IGW) is a horizontally-scaled, redundant VPC component that enables communication between VPC instances and the internet.

questions.question: A platform team manages 40 AWS resources across 3 environments. They want to declare the entire stack as code in JSON or YAML files, version-control it, do change-set previews before applying, and roll back on failure. Which AWS service is the native infrastructure-as-code engine?
options: Elastic Beanstalk — PaaS deployment, not a general IaC engine
OpsWorks — Chef/Puppet config management, not declarative IaC
AWS CloudFormation — declarative JSON/YAML templates, change sets, drift detection, rollback
Systems Manager — operational management, not template-based IaC
questions.explanation: AWS CloudFormation allows you to define AWS infrastructure as JSON or YAML templates and deploy it in a repeatable, automated way.

questions.question: A team needs to (a) register a `.com` domain, (b) host an authoritative DNS zone, (c) route users by geolocation/latency/weighted policies, (d) integrate health checks for failover. Which AWS service?
options: Network Load Balancer — L4 LB, not DNS
Amazon CloudFront — CDN, not DNS or registrar
AWS VPN — connectivity service, unrelated
Amazon Route 53 — authoritative DNS + domain registrar + advanced routing policies + health checks
questions.explanation: Route 53 is AWS's scalable DNS service. It routes users to applications, supports health checks, and offers routing policies like latency, geolocation, and failover.

questions.question: A team has medical imaging files that are accessed about 4× per year but, when accessed, must be retrievable in MILLISECONDS (not hours). They want to pay less than S3 Standard storage rates. Which S3 storage class fits?
options: S3 Standard-IA — same millisecond retrieval as Standard at a lower storage rate, with a per-GB retrieval fee — designed for infrequent access
S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval — minutes-to-hours retrieval, cheaper but does not meet the millisecond requirement
S3 Standard — cheapest per retrieval but most expensive per GB stored, ill-suited for infrequent access
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — hours retrieval, cheapest storage, definitely not millisecond
questions.explanation: S3 Standard-IA is for data accessed less frequently but needs immediate access when required. Lower storage cost than S3 Standard but retrieval fee applies.

questions.question: A security architect drafts IAM policy for a new EC2 role. The role's job is to read ONE specific S3 bucket. Best practice says grant nothing beyond that exact need — not full S3, not even read on all buckets. Which IAM principle is this?
options: Least privilege — grant the MINIMUM permissions needed for the task
Broad admin access — explicitly the opposite of best practice
Shared IAM user across the team — anti-pattern; no audit per person
Long-lived access keys on users — anti-pattern; prefer assumable roles
questions.explanation: The principle of least privilege means granting only the permissions necessary to perform a task — nothing more. This minimizes the blast radius of compromised credentials.

questions.question: A web-server EC2 instance must accept HTTPS (TCP 443) from anywhere and SSH (TCP 22) only from the office IP. The control is a STATEFUL allow-only firewall attached to the instance's ENI, where outbound replies are auto-permitted by state. Which AWS control is this?
options: Network ACL — STATELESS, subnet-level, allow AND deny rules
EC2 Security Group — STATEFUL, instance-level (per ENI), ALLOW-only rules (no explicit deny)
IAM group — controls administrator actions, not network flows
VPC route table entry — controls routing, not packet filtering
questions.explanation: Security Groups are stateful (return traffic automatically allowed) instance-level firewalls. You define allow rules only — there are no deny rules. Compare with Network ACLs which are stateless and subnet-level.

questions.question: An architect compares two VPC firewall constructs: (A) stateful, attached to ENIs, ALLOW-only, evaluates rules together; (B) stateless, attached to subnets, can ALLOW or DENY, evaluates rules in numbered order. Which mapping is correct?
options: They are identical, only console-UI differs — false
Security Group = stateful, instance-level, allow-only. NACL = stateless, subnet-level, allow + deny ordered
NACLs are instance-level; SGs are subnet-level — reversed
SGs evaluate outbound only; NACLs evaluate inbound only — false; both apply both directions
questions.explanation: SG: stateful (return traffic auto-allowed), instance level, allow rules only, evaluated as a whole. NACL: stateless (return traffic needs explicit rule), subnet level, ordered allow/deny rules. instance-level, allow-only rules. Network ACLs: stateless, subnet-level, allow AND deny rules

questions.question: A relational database on EC2 needs PERSISTENT block storage that survives instance stop/start AND can be reattached to a different instance in the same AZ. The storage must be a /dev/sdX block device the OS formats with a filesystem. Which AWS storage primitive fits?
options: Amazon S3 — object storage with REST API, not a block device
Amazon EBS — persistent block storage volume that outlives the instance and can be detached/reattached
Amazon EFS — POSIX NFS file system (file, not block)
EC2 Instance Store — ephemeral local SSD, lost on stop/terminate
questions.explanation: EBS (Elastic Block Store) provides persistent block storage volumes attached to EC2. Unlike instance store, EBS persists after instance stop/terminate and can be detached/reattached.

questions.question: A fleet of 12 EC2 web servers in 3 AZs must SHARE one writable filesystem so user uploads written by one server are immediately visible to the others. The filesystem must be POSIX with NFS-mount semantics, scale storage automatically, and be regional (multi-AZ). Which AWS service?
options: Amazon EFS — elastic NFS file system, multi-AZ, mount across many EC2 instances simultaneously
Amazon EBS — single-instance block volume (multi-attach is limited and not a multi-AZ NFS)
Amazon S3 — object storage, not a POSIX filesystem with concurrent NFS mounts
AWS Storage Gateway tape archive — VTL, unrelated
questions.explanation: EFS (Elastic File System) is a managed NFS file system that can be mounted to multiple EC2 instances across Availability Zones simultaneously. Unlike EBS which attaches to one instance.

questions.question: EC2 instances in a PRIVATE subnet need OUTBOUND internet access (e.g., to call SaaS APIs and pull OS updates) WITHOUT being directly reachable from the internet inbound. Which VPC component provides outbound-only NAT for private subnets?
options: VPC Peering — links two VPCs privately; no internet path
NAT Gateway — managed NAT service: private-subnet outbound to internet via Elastic IP, NO inbound
Internet Gateway — bidirectional ingress/egress, NOT outbound-only
Virtual Private Gateway (VGW) — terminates IPsec VPN tunnels from on-prem; this is a different service from NAT GW
questions.explanation: NAT Gateway = managed outbound-only NAT for private subnets, billed per hour + per GB. Internet Gateway = bidirectional. Virtual Private Gateway = IPsec VPN termination (a completely different service). PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked VPN termination as the NAT GW definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A web tier has 6 EC2 instances serving HTTPS. A new release introduces autoscaling — at peak the fleet may grow to 30, at trough shrink to 3. The team needs a managed service that automatically registers/deregisters scaling instances and distributes inbound HTTPS requests with health checks. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudFront — edge CDN for cached content, not a back-end load distributor
Amazon RDS read-replica — database scaling, not HTTPS distribution
Amazon Route 53 weighted records — DNS-level distribution, no per-request layer-7 health checking like ELB
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes inbound to EC2 / containers / IP / Lambda targets with health checks
questions.explanation: ELB distributes traffic across multiple targets. ALB (Application) = Layer 7/HTTP, NLB (Network) = Layer 4/TCP, GLB (Gateway) = Layer 3 for third-party appliances. Integrates with Auto Scaling.

questions.question: A bucket holding critical compliance docs is at risk of accidental overwrite/delete by the application or by an admin. The team wants to retain a HISTORY of every object version, recover prior versions, and undelete tombstoned objects. Which S3 feature?
options: Bucket-creation order counter — not a real S3 feature
Bucket-policy history — IAM history, not object history
S3 Versioning — retains all versions of every object; PUT and DELETE create new versions / delete markers, allowing recovery
S3 Object-level CloudTrail — different surface; CloudTrail audits API calls but does not retain object content
questions.explanation: S3 Versioning stores all versions of an object including writes and deletes. Enables recovery from accidental overwrites/deletes. Can be used with Lifecycle policies to manage costs.

questions.question: An ops team wants automated recommendations across COST (idle resources, RI coverage), PERFORMANCE (under-provisioned instances), SECURITY (open SGs, root MFA), FAULT TOLERANCE (no Multi-AZ), and SERVICE LIMITS (approaching quotas) — refreshed continuously and surfaced in the console. Which AWS service?
options: External pen-test firm — manual, not a continuous AWS service
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — narrower (policy-grant analysis), not the 5-pillar recommendations
AWS Organizations — multi-account billing/governance, not service-level recommendations
AWS Trusted Advisor — automated checks across 5 pillars (cost / performance / security / fault tolerance / service limits)
questions.explanation: Trusted Advisor inspects your AWS environment and provides actionable recommendations. Basic checks (free): S3 bucket permissions, MFA on root account. Full checks require Business or Enterprise support.

questions.question: A new AWS account holder is reading the Free Tier offer. AWS publishes three categories: ALWAYS-FREE services, 12-MONTH free usage for new accounts, and SHORT-TRIAL free for specific services. Which describes the Free Tier correctly?
options: Every AWS service is offered free below a usage cap — false
Free Tier covers EC2 only — false
Limited free usage for 12 months on NEW accounts PLUS always-free and short-trial offers across services — the documented composition
AWS Activate startup credits — different program (separate from Free Tier)
questions.explanation: AWS Free Tier includes: 12-month free (new accounts) — e.g., 750hr/month EC2 t2.micro; Always free — e.g., 1M Lambda requests/month; Trial — e.g., 2 months Amazon Redshift.

questions.question: A team needs a managed relational database with: (a) MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatibility (zero application change), (b) auto-scaling storage up to 128 TB, (c) up to 15 low-latency cross-AZ read replicas, (d) standard AWS billing per second. Which managed RDS engine fits ALL four?
options: DynamoDB — NoSQL key-value, NOT MySQL/PostgreSQL wire-compatible
ElastiCache for Redis — in-memory key-value, not a relational engine
Amazon Aurora (MySQL- or PostgreSQL-compatible) — managed RDBMS with auto-scaling storage and up to 15 replicas
Redshift — columnar data warehouse for analytics, not OLTP RDBMS
questions.explanation: Aurora is AWS's cloud-native relational database. It auto-scales storage, replicates across 3 AZs with 6 copies, and offers serverless options. Fully managed within RDS.

questions.question: A Lambda function must read from DynamoDB and write to S3. The team wants AWS BEST PRACTICE for credentials: NO long-lived access keys baked into the function code or env vars; AWS auto-injects temporary credentials when the function runs. Which IAM construct does this?
options: IAM User with access keys — long-lived, anti-pattern for compute identity
IAM Role assumed via STS — short-lived temporary credentials auto-vended to the Lambda execution environment
IAM Group — a collection of users, cannot itself execute code or assume permissions
IAM Policy document — describes permissions, but is attached to a principal (user/role/group), not used directly
questions.explanation: IAM Roles are assumable identities with permissions. EC2 instances, Lambda functions, and cross-account users assume roles. No static credentials — uses temporary security tokens via STS.

questions.question: A web tier writes 'order placed' events to a backend that must NOT lose messages even if the consumer is down for hours. The consumer is a worker fleet that PULLS messages, processes them, and explicitly deletes them. Which AWS service fits this decoupling pattern?
options: Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — streaming with shard partitioning, real-time analytics use case
AWS Step Functions — state-machine orchestration, not a pull-based queue
Amazon SNS — pub/sub fan-out, push-based, no pull-and-delete semantics
Amazon SQS — managed pull-based message queue with visibility timeout and explicit delete on success
questions.explanation: SQS (Simple Queue Service) decouples microservices by providing a durable message buffer. Producers send messages; consumers poll and process them. Prevents data loss if a consumer fails.

questions.question: An architect compares two AWS messaging services: (A) pull-based; consumer reads, processes, and deletes; one-to-one with the worker fleet. (B) push-based pub/sub; topic broadcasts to many subscribers (Lambda, SQS, email, SMS, HTTPS). Which is which?
options: They are functionally identical — false
SNS retains durably; SQS does not — false (SQS is the queue with durability)
SQS = pull-based queue for decoupling; SNS = push-based pub/sub for fan-out
SQS is for email; SNS is for application queuing — reversed and incorrect
questions.explanation: SQS: one consumer polls messages from a queue (point-to-point). SNS (Simple Notification Service): one message fan-out to multiple subscribers (email, SQS, Lambda, HTTP) simultaneously.

questions.question: A 300 TB media archive sits in an on-prem data centre with a 1 Gbps internet uplink. Online transfer would take weeks. AWS offers a physical appliance shipped to the customer site for offline bulk transfer (encrypted at rest, returned for ingest). Which service?
options: AWS Disaster Recovery — orchestrates failover, no physical appliance
S3 Glacier Deep Archive — cold storage class, not a transfer appliance
Amazon CloudFront — edge CDN, unrelated
AWS Snowball / Snowball Edge — rugged physical appliance for offline bulk dataset transfer
questions.explanation: AWS Snowball is a secure, physical appliance for offline data migration. 80TB capacity. Snowball Edge adds compute. Snowmobile is a 100PB truck for exabyte migrations.

questions.question: A small dev team wants to deploy a Node.js web app to AWS without configuring the underlying EC2 / LB / autoscaling / health-checks themselves. They upload the source, AWS provisions everything based on the platform, scales it, and updates it. Which AWS service fits?
options: Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes control plane; team still owns workloads + scaling configuration
Amazon ECR — container image registry only, not a PaaS
AWS CDK — IaC tool that synthesises CloudFormation; not a runtime
AWS Elastic Beanstalk — PaaS that provisions EC2 + LB + autoscaling + health behind a simple deploy
questions.explanation: Elastic Beanstalk is a PaaS that deploys web apps (Java, .NET, PHP, Node.js, Python, Ruby, Go, Docker). You upload code; Beanstalk handles the infrastructure. You still control the underlying resources.

questions.question: All web traffic must be encrypted in transit. The certificate that proves the server's identity and enables TLS handshakes must be (a) trusted by every modern browser, (b) issued / renewed automatically by AWS at no cost, (c) usable on ALB + CloudFront + API GW. Which AWS service issues these public TLS certs?
options: AWS Shield Advanced — DDoS protection, no certs
AWS WAF — L7 rules, no certs
AWS Global Accelerator — anycast routing, no certs
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) — free public TLS cert issuance and renewal for ALB / CloudFront / API GW
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS/SSL for encryption. AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) provisions and manages free public SSL/TLS certificates for use with ELB, CloudFront, and API Gateway.

questions.question: An analytics team runs SQL queries over 500 TB of clickstream data. The workload is read-heavy, scans large columns of a few facts at a time, joins to dimension tables, and benefits from columnar compression + MPP (massively parallel processing). Which AWS service?
options: ElastiCache — in-memory key-value, not analytics
RDS for MySQL/Postgres — OLTP relational, not petabyte columnar
Amazon Redshift — managed columnar data warehouse with MPP and Spectrum-to-S3 for analytics
DynamoDB — NoSQL key-value, not relational analytics
questions.explanation: Redshift is AWS's managed data warehouse for analytics (OLAP). Uses columnar storage and MPP (Massively Parallel Processing) to run complex analytical queries across petabytes of data.

questions.question: A compliance team needs the AWS service that: (a) takes a snapshot of every resource's CONFIGURATION over time, (b) evaluates each snapshot against rules (e.g., 'S3 bucket must have versioning enabled'), (c) surfaces drift with timeline + non-compliant flag. Which service?
options: AWS Systems Manager — manages running EC2 (patching, sessions), not RM-config history
AWS Config — records resource configuration history and evaluates against rules
AWS CodeDeploy — deploys application code to EC2 / on-prem / Lambda; not config recording
AWS IAM Access Analyzer — analyses IAM grants, not resource config history
questions.explanation: AWS Config is the configuration-recording / rule-evaluation service. CodeDeploy deploys application code. Systems Manager is run-time admin. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked CodeDeploy's description as Config) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A public-facing web tier is hit with a sustained Layer-3/4 volumetric DDoS (SYN floods, UDP reflection). The customer wants automatic, no-config-required L3/L4 DDoS protection AT NO ADDITIONAL CHARGE; for the higher tier (cost-protection guarantees, DDoS Response Team access) they're willing to pay extra. Which service provides this?
options: AWS Shield (Standard = free, Advanced = paid) — L3/L4 DDoS protection with the cost-protection tier described
AWS WAF — Layer-7 HTTP rules, not L3/L4 volumetric protection
AWS KMS — key management, unrelated to DDoS
AWS Certificate Manager — TLS-cert lifecycle, unrelated to DDoS
questions.explanation: AWS Shield Standard: free, automatic DDoS protection for all AWS customers. Shield Advanced: paid, enhanced protection for EC2, ELB, CloudFront, Route 53 with the DDoS Response Team (DRT) and financial protection.

questions.question: A telemetry pipeline must ingest 1 million events/sec from IoT devices, retain them ordered for 24-168 hours, and let multiple consumers replay the stream (Lambda, Firehose to S3, Analytics with windowing). Which AWS service is the streaming primitive?
options: Amazon RDS — managed relational database, NOT a streaming primitive
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — managed, shard-partitioned, ordered event stream with multiple consumers and replay
Amazon S3 — durable object store; can be a Kinesis SINK but not the streaming primitive itself
Amazon SQS — pull-based queue, not the streaming-ordered-replayable model
questions.explanation: Kinesis Data Streams is the streaming primitive: shard-partitioned, ordered within a shard, retention 24-168 hours, multiple consumers can replay. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked RDS as the streaming answer) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An e-commerce ALB-fronted app is being probed with SQLi and XSS payloads. The team wants Layer-7 HTTP request inspection that blocks known bad patterns (OWASP Top 10 managed rule groups) and rate-limits abusive sources — without code change. Which AWS service?
options: Site-to-Site VPN — encrypted tunnels, not L7 inspection
VPC Flow Log ML detection — flow-record analytics, not L7 inspection
AWS Network Firewall — L3/L4 stateful firewall at VPC boundary, not L7
AWS WAF — L7 HTTP inspection with managed rule groups for SQLi / XSS / bad actors; rate-limit rules
questions.explanation: AWS WAF filters web traffic to CloudFront, ALB, API Gateway, and AppSync. You create rules to allow/block requests based on IP, headers, body content, or SQL/XSS patterns.

questions.question: A read-heavy product-detail page has 70% of requests hitting the database for the SAME 10 000 hot keys. The team wants to put a sub-millisecond key-value cache IN FRONT of the database with TTL-based invalidation. Which AWS service?
options: RDS read replicas — relational scaling but not sub-ms key-value
Amazon ElastiCache (Redis / Memcached) — managed in-memory cache for sub-ms reads in front of the DB
Amazon CloudFront — CDN edge cache for HTTP, not a key-value DB front
DAX — DynamoDB-specific accelerator, not generic
questions.explanation: ElastiCache reduces database load by caching frequent queries in memory. Redis supports persistence, pub/sub, sorted sets. Memcached is simpler, multi-threaded. Both offer microsecond read latency.

questions.question: A container team wants to run Docker workloads on AWS without managing any EC2 worker nodes — AWS picks the underlying compute, scales it, patches it. The team only declares CPU / memory per task. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon EKS with managed node groups — managed K8s control plane, but workers are still EC2 the customer manages
ECS on the EC2 launch type — customer manages the EC2 worker fleet
AWS Fargate — serverless container runtime; AWS owns the underlying compute
AWS Lambda — function-as-a-service for code, not arbitrary container workloads (except via container-image runtime, narrower)
questions.explanation: AWS Fargate is a serverless compute engine for containers (used with ECS or EKS). No EC2 instances to manage — you define CPU/memory requirements, and AWS handles the infrastructure.

questions.question: A multi-region application wants ANYCAST IP entry points: users globally connect to a single static IP that the AWS network routes over its backbone to the closest healthy regional endpoint, with sub-second failover on regional health degradation. Which service?
options: Amazon CloudFront — caching CDN, not a static-IP backbone-routed accelerator
Amazon Route 53 — DNS-based routing, not anycast IP entry
AWS Global Accelerator — two static anycast IPs that route over AWS backbone to closest healthy Regional endpoint
Application Load Balancer — regional L7 LB, not global
questions.explanation: Global Accelerator uses AWS's private global network (not the internet) to route traffic to the optimal regional endpoint, reducing latency and improving failover for global applications.

questions.question: An RDS engineer compares two HA-vs-scaling options: (A) a synchronous standby in a different AZ that the engine auto-fails-over to on primary failure; (B) asynchronous COPY replicas in the same or other Region that take read traffic to scale OUT reads. Which mapping is correct?
options: They are functionally interchangeable — false
Read Replicas are for point-in-time backup — false; automated backups are a separate feature
Multi-AZ = synchronous standby for HA failover; Read Replicas = asynchronous read-scaling replicas
Multi-AZ is for cross-Region DR — false; Multi-AZ is in-region; cross-Region is Read Replicas or Aurora Global
questions.explanation: Multi-AZ: synchronous standby in different AZ for failover HA — automatic failover ~1-2min. Read Replicas: asynchronous copies for read scaling — promotes manually for DR. Both can exist simultaneously.

questions.question: An auditor asks for the customer's most recent SOC 2 Type 2, PCI-DSS AOC, and ISO 27001 certificate from AWS. The customer needs a self-service portal that issues download-on-demand attestations. Which AWS service?
options: AWS CodeCommit — Git repo, no compliance reports
Amazon ECR — container image registry, no compliance reports
AWS Artifact — self-service portal for AWS compliance reports (SOC, PCI-DSS, ISO 27001, etc.)
AWS CodeBuild — CI build service, unrelated
questions.explanation: AWS Artifact provides on-demand access to AWS's compliance documentation: SOC 1/2/3, PCI DSS, ISO 27001, HIPAA reports, and agreements. Useful for enterprise compliance and audits.

questions.question: A compliance team wants S3 buckets continuously scanned to find objects containing PII / PHI / credentials. The scanner must classify with ML, emit findings into Security Hub, and not require shipping bucket contents externally. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon GuardDuty — VPC Flow / DNS / CloudTrail anomaly detection, NOT S3 content classification
AWS Network Firewall — L3/L4 firewall, not S3 content scan
Amazon Macie — managed ML-based sensitive-data discovery on S3 (PII, credentials, etc.)
AWS KMS — key management, not content scanning
questions.explanation: Macie uses machine learning to automatically discover and protect sensitive data (PII, financial data) in S3 buckets, identifying overly permissive access or sensitive data exposure.

questions.question: A SOC wants AUTOMATED, MACHINE-LEARNING-BASED threat detection on AWS API activity (CloudTrail), VPC Flow Logs, and Route 53 DNS. The service must flag known IoCs, anomalous behaviour, and cryptocurrency-mining EC2s — with NO agent on instances. Which AWS service?
options: AWS WAF — L7 HTTP rules, not behavioural detection
Endpoint AV on EC2 — agent-based, the question excludes that
Inline VPC IDS appliance — agent-free at instance but not the named AWS-managed service
Amazon GuardDuty — agentless ML detection across CloudTrail + VPC Flow + DNS, integrated with Security Hub
questions.explanation: GuardDuty uses ML and threat intelligence to detect unusual API calls, unauthorized deployments, cryptocurrency mining, and compromised instances — with no agents to install.

questions.question: A FinOps analyst wants to (a) chart historical spend per service / per tag / per linked account, (b) compare last quarter to this, (c) drill into cost spikes. The analysis is over ALREADY-INCURRED costs, not estimates. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Pricing Calculator — pre-deploy estimates, not historical
AWS Budgets — threshold alerts on actual / forecast, not deep historical drill-down
AWS Cost Explorer — visualises and analyses actual AWS cost + usage history with grouping/filtering
AWS Artifact — compliance report portal, not cost
questions.explanation: Cost Explorer lets you analyze historical cost trends, identify cost drivers, forecast future spend, and find optimization opportunities with detailed filtering and charting.

questions.question: A company has 40+ AWS accounts. They want one place to: (a) create new accounts, (b) cluster them into OUs, (c) apply guardrails via Service Control Policies, (d) consolidate billing into one invoice. Which AWS service?
options: AWS IAM Identity Center — workforce SSO, not multi-account governance
AWS Migration Hub — migration tracking, unrelated
AWS Organizations — central multi-account management, OUs, SCPs, consolidated billing
AWS Auto Scaling — capacity scaling, unrelated
questions.explanation: AWS Organizations enables centralized management of multiple AWS accounts: consolidated billing (volume discounts), Service Control Policies to restrict account permissions, and account grouping in OUs.

questions.question: Inside AWS Organizations, a permission GUARDRAIL applies at the OU or account level. It can DENY (or filter) what any IAM principal — including the account's root user — is allowed to do. It does NOT grant permissions, only caps them. Which construct is this?
options: An IAM identity-based policy attached to users / groups / roles — grants permissions, not a guardrail cap
A Service Control Policy (SCP) at the OU or account scope — the GUARDRAIL that caps maximum permissions
A VPC-level network policy filtering subnet traffic — networking, not IAM
A CloudFormation template that provisions stacks — IaC, not a permission guardrail
questions.explanation: SCPs are the AWS Organizations guardrail: they cap (deny / filter) the maximum permissions for IAM principals in the targeted OU / account, including the account's root user. They never GRANT — they only restrict. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked CloudFormation, which is IaC) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A SaaS vendor wants to publish their product as an AMI that AWS customers can deploy, with metered billing on hourly or per-API-call basis, with consolidated invoicing through the customer's AWS bill. Which AWS feature publishes/buys SaaS, AMIs, and containers?
options: AWS Marketplace — catalogue of 3rd-party AMIs / SaaS / containers / data products with flexible billing options
AWS Marketplace for branded AWS hardware — not a thing
AWS Careers portal — for AWS job openings, unrelated to product distribution
AWS RI Marketplace — secondary market for selling Reserved Instances, much narrower
questions.explanation: AWS Marketplace lets customers find, subscribe to, and deploy third-party software that runs on AWS. Includes security, networking, data, ML, and business intelligence tools with flexible billing.

questions.question: A cloud-101 lecture defines a property as: 'resources can be ADDED or REMOVED automatically in response to demand signals, and you pay only for actual usage'. This contrasts with the on-prem paradigm of static, over-provisioned peak capacity. Which cloud property is this?
options: Manual capacity stretching of on-prem hardware — not elasticity
Automatic scaling up AND down with demand, paying for actual usage — the textbook elasticity property
Annual long-horizon capacity planning — opposite of dynamic elasticity
Static fixed allocation reserved for peak load — the on-prem model, opposite of cloud elasticity
questions.explanation: Elasticity = dynamically scale resources with demand + pay for actual usage. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked static peak allocation as elasticity, which is exactly backwards) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An app-sec team wants ongoing CVE scanning of running EC2 instances (kernel + installed packages) AND of Lambda function dependencies, with findings emitted into Security Hub. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Cost Explorer — cost, unrelated
AWS Config — config recording, not CVE
AWS Artifact — compliance docs, not scanning
Amazon Inspector — automated vuln assessment of EC2 / Lambda / ECR with CVE catalogue + Security Hub integration
questions.explanation: Amazon Inspector automatically scans for known CVEs in running EC2/Lambda workloads and checks for unintended network accessibility (e.g., open SSH to 0.0.0.0/0), providing prioritized findings.

questions.question: An auditor asks AWS who is responsible for: (1) the physical security of the data centre, (2) hypervisor patching, (3) the customer's EC2 guest OS patching, (4) the customer's application data encryption. Which mapping is correct under the Shared Responsibility Model?
options: Customer owns ALL four items — incorrect, AWS owns the foundation
AWS owns ALL four items — incorrect, customer owns IN-cloud responsibilities
Mapping varies by support tier — incorrect, the model is fixed, not support-tier-dependent
AWS = security OF the cloud (DC, hardware, hypervisor, network); Customer = security IN the cloud (guest OS, IAM, data, application config)
questions.explanation: AWS: physical security, data center facilities, networking hardware, hypervisor, and managed service infrastructure. Customer: everything they put in the cloud — data encryption, IAM, OS patching on EC2, network config.

questions.question: A platform team wants ONE place to collect logs from: EC2 (via agent), Lambda (auto-stream), ECS containers, on-prem servers (agent), VPC Flow Logs. The destination must let them query with a SQL-like language, set retention, and create metric filters. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudWatch Logs — central log ingestion + Logs Insights queries + retention + metric filters
Amazon RDS — relational database, not log aggregation
AWS CodeCommit — Git repo, not logs
S3 server-access logs — only S3 access events, narrow
questions.explanation: CloudWatch Logs centralizes logs from any source. You can create metric filters (count errors in logs), set alarms, and analyze with CloudWatch Logs Insights queries.

questions.question: An architect designing for high availability must distinguish two AWS scope concepts: (1) a geographic area containing multiple isolated data-centre clusters connected by low-latency fibre, (2) one or more of those data-centre clusters in distinct power/cooling/network failure domains. Which mapping is correct?
options: Regions and AZs are interchangeable terms — false
AZs are global; Regions are facility-scoped — reversed
Region = geographic area containing 3+ Availability Zones; AZ = one or more physically isolated data centres connected by low-latency private fibre
Regions hold object storage exclusively; AZs hold compute exclusively — false
questions.explanation: A Region (e.g., us-east-1) is a geographic cluster of AZs. An AZ (e.g., us-east-1a) is one or more data centers with independent infrastructure. Multi-AZ deployments protect against single data center failure.

questions.question: A backend team builds 30 REST and WebSocket endpoints. They want a managed service that handles: throttling, API keys, usage plans, JWT auth, request/response mapping, canary deployments, and CloudFront-edge presence. Which AWS service?
options: An on-prem network gateway device — not a managed API service
Amazon CloudFront — caching CDN, not an API management plane
Amazon Route 53 — DNS, not API
Amazon API Gateway — managed REST + WebSocket API frontend with throttling / auth / keys / canaries
questions.explanation: API Gateway is the front door for backend services (Lambda, EC2, HTTP endpoints). It handles authentication, throttling, caching, monitoring, versioning, and API key management.

questions.question: A backend must orchestrate this flow: (1) start a Lambda, (2) wait for human approval, (3) run a Glue ETL job, (4) on success notify SNS, (5) on failure invoke a different Lambda. The flow is long-running, has retries with exponential backoff, and is auditable. Which service?
options: AWS CodePipeline — CI/CD release workflows, not a general-purpose state machine
AWS DMS — database migration, unrelated
AWS Batch — runs containerised batch jobs, no human-approval orchestration
AWS Step Functions — serverless orchestration as JSON state machines with retries, human-approval, parallel branches, and visual flows
questions.explanation: Step Functions orchestrates distributed applications as state machines with visual workflows. Coordinates Lambda, ECS, DynamoDB, SNS, SQS, and more with built-in error handling and retries.

questions.question: An architect maps a workload's improvement to one of the six Well-Architected pillars. The work focuses on rightsizing instance families, buying Savings Plans, deleting idle resources, lifecycle-tiering S3. Which pillar?
options: Operational Excellence — ops process, not cost
Cost Optimisation — rightsizing, RIs/SP, eliminating idle, tier-by-access
Reliability — recovery from failure, not cost
Performance Efficiency — using resources efficiently for performance, related but distinct
questions.explanation: Cost Optimization pillar focuses on avoiding unnecessary costs: right-sizing instances, using Reserved/Spot pricing, deleting unused resources, and understanding spend. All 6 pillars: Operational Excellence, Security, Reliability, Performance Efficiency, Cost Optimization, Sustainability.

questions.question: An app must retrieve an RDS password at runtime that auto-rotates every 30 days, encrypts at rest with a customer-managed KMS key, and emits a CloudTrail event on each retrieval. Which AWS service stores and rotates this secret?
options: Browser-based consumer password manager — not for application secrets
S3 default encryption — encrypts objects, doesn't rotate or vend secrets
IAM password policy — governs IAM-user passwords, not application secrets
AWS Secrets Manager — KMS-encrypted secret store with built-in rotation, CloudTrail audit, and language-SDK retrieval
questions.explanation: Secrets Manager stores secrets securely and can automatically rotate them (e.g., RDS passwords every 30 days) without application downtime. Applications retrieve secrets via API — no hardcoded credentials.

questions.question: An architect new to AWS asks where to find AWS's prescriptive best-practice guidance, organised into pillars that an architecture review can score against (with detailed lenses for serverless, machine-learning, SaaS, IoT). Which official AWS resource is this?
options: Well-Architected Framework — best-practice guidance across the 6 pillars (Operations, Security, Reliability, Performance, Cost, Sustainability) plus lenses
AWS Pricing Catalogue — public price list, not best practices
AWS Certification Blueprint — exam-prep guide, not a design framework
AWS Solution Architect Deployment Checklist — there is no such named official artefact
questions.explanation: The Well-Architected Framework helps architects build secure, high-performing, resilient, and efficient infrastructure. Use the Well-Architected Tool in the AWS console for free architectural reviews.

questions.question: A team wants to run ad-hoc SQL queries DIRECTLY against parquet/CSV/JSON files stored in S3, with NO database to provision, billed per TB scanned. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon RDS — managed relational DB; data must be loaded in, not queried in-place on S3
Amazon Athena — serverless interactive SQL directly on S3 data, billed per TB scanned, no infra to manage
AWS Database Migration Service (DMS) — moves DBs to AWS, not in-place SQL on S3
AWS Glue — ETL service; the data catalog feeds Athena but is not the query engine itself
questions.explanation: Athena is serverless ANSI SQL over data in S3 using Presto/Trino. Billed per TB scanned. Uses the Glue Data Catalog. DMS is a migration tool. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A team wants a managed ETL service to (a) crawl source data, build a data catalog with schemas, (b) author and run Spark / Python jobs that transform S3 / RDS / Redshift data, (c) all serverless. Which AWS service?
options: VPC Reachability Analyzer — networking diagnostic, unrelated
AWS CodePipeline — CI/CD pipeline, not data ETL
AWS Glue — serverless ETL with Crawlers + Data Catalog + Spark/Python jobs
Amazon Kinesis Data Streams — real-time streaming primitive, not batch ETL with a catalog
questions.explanation: AWS Glue provides: Data Catalog (metadata repository for all your data sources), ETL jobs (serverless Spark-based transformations), and Crawlers (auto-discover schema from S3, RDS, etc.).

questions.question: A team wants to run Docker workloads with AWS-native orchestration (no Kubernetes). They want to pick the underlying compute: either EC2 (customer-managed) or Fargate (serverless). Which AWS service is the orchestrator?
options: Amazon ECS — AWS-native container orchestrator; runs tasks on EC2 launch type OR Fargate launch type
Amazon EKS — managed Kubernetes; explicitly Kubernetes, not AWS-native ECS
Amazon ECR — image registry, not orchestrator
EC2 Auto Scaling Group — generic VM scaling, not container orchestration
questions.explanation: ECS manages containerized applications. EC2 launch type: you manage the underlying EC2 fleet. Fargate: serverless — no EC2 management. Amazon ECR stores container images. ECS integrates with ALB, IAM, CloudWatch.

questions.question: A pre-baked OS image with a specific Linux distro, kernel version, pre-installed nginx + Python venv, and security-hardened config is published as a reusable EC2 image. Launching a new EC2 from this image gives you that EXACT environment. What is this template called?
options: AWS Management Console — the browser admin UI, NOT an EC2 launch image
An Amazon Machine Image (AMI) — template (root volume + launch permissions + block-device mapping) that EC2 uses to provision instances
An asymmetric key-pair — for SSH, not the OS image template
A VPC template — defines a network, not an OS image
questions.explanation: An AMI is the EC2 launch template: it bundles a root volume snapshot, launch permissions, and a block-device mapping. AMI ≠ the browser management console. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: A SOC engineer needs the AUTHORITATIVE record of every API call against the AWS account: who (principal), what (action), when (timestamp), from where (IP, user-agent), with what (request parameters), result (status). The service is tenant-wide and immutable by default. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon VPC Reachability Analyzer — network reachability, unrelated
AWS CloudTrail — tenant-wide, immutable, default-on log of every AWS API call with caller identity, time, IP, parameters
Amazon CloudWatch Logs — general application/system log aggregation surface; NOT the per-API audit trail
VPC Flow Logs — packet-flow telemetry, not control-plane audit
questions.explanation: CloudTrail is the tenant-wide audit log of AWS API calls. CloudWatch Logs aggregates application/system logs but is NOT the API audit trail. PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (mislabelled CloudTrail as 'general log aggregation') — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An IaC team compares two AWS provisioning tools: (A) declarative templates in YAML or JSON; resources, parameters, mappings, outputs. (B) imperative TypeScript / Python / Java / Go / .NET code that SYNTHESISES into (A)'s template format. Which is which?
options: They are the same product — false
CloudFormation = declarative YAML/JSON templates; CDK = imperative code in mainstream languages that synthesises CFN templates
CDK is container-only — false; CDK provisions any AWS resource type
CloudFormation is deprecated — false; CDK builds on top of it
questions.explanation: CloudFormation is the foundational IaC service — template-based. CDK allows writing infrastructure using familiar languages with OOP constructs, then synthesizes CloudFormation. Higher level of abstraction.

questions.question: An IAM principal is granted `s3:GetObject` by an attached identity policy AND explicitly denied `s3:GetObject` by a resource policy on the same bucket. AWS's IAM evaluation logic says one rule about Allow vs Deny is absolute. Which is it?
options: Explicit Allow wins over explicit Deny — false
Whichever policy attached first wins — false
More specific match wins regardless of effect — false
Explicit Deny ALWAYS wins; with no matching statement the request is implicitly denied (default-deny)
questions.explanation: AWS IAM policy evaluation: Any explicit Deny wins regardless of any Allow. This enables denying specific actions even for admins. All requests start as implicitly denied — Allows must be explicitly granted.

questions.question: A company moves 8 Gbps of sustained traffic between an on-prem DC and AWS. They need (a) consistent, predictable throughput (not best-effort internet), (b) lower egress pricing than internet, (c) data must NOT traverse the public internet. Which AWS service?
options: Site-to-Site VPN — IPsec over the public internet; doesn't meet bypass-internet
Internet peering — still internet
Internet transit service — still internet
AWS Direct Connect — dedicated physical fibre link (1/10/100 Gbps) into AWS, bypassing the public internet
questions.explanation: Direct Connect provides 1Gbps or 10Gbps dedicated connections via AWS Direct Connect Partners. Unlike VPN, no internet fluctuations. Good for large data transfers, hybrid cloud, and compliance requirements.

questions.question: A team needs a HIERARCHICAL key/value config + secret store for app config: dev/prod/region scoping via the path key, AT REST encryption via KMS for SecureString entries, version history per parameter, and a generous free tier. Which AWS service fits (without Secrets Manager's automatic rotation features)?
options: AWS Secrets Manager — has rotation, but PAID per secret; the question asks for the free / config-store alternative
S3 bucket storing config files — works but no native KMS+versioning+hierarchy semantics for params
EC2 fleet manager — operational, not config storage
Systems Manager Parameter Store — hierarchical, KMS-encrypted SecureString, version history, free standard tier
questions.explanation: Parameter Store stores config data (DB strings, feature flags, AMI IDs) hierarchically (e.g., /prod/db/password). Free for standard parameters. SecureString type encrypts with KMS. Alternative to hardcoded config.

questions.question: An e-commerce service needs a NoSQL database with: (a) single-digit ms latency at any scale, (b) no servers to provision, (c) horizontal partitioning by item key, (d) global tables (multi-region active-active), (e) on-demand or provisioned capacity. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon RDS Aurora — relational, not key-value NoSQL
Amazon Redshift — columnar analytics warehouse, not low-latency OLTP
Amazon DynamoDB — serverless NoSQL key-value + document, single-digit ms, partition-key sharded, Global Tables
Amazon Neptune — graph DB, different shape
questions.explanation: DynamoDB: zero administration, auto-scales from 0 to millions of requests/second. Single-digit millisecond latency. Choose when: high throughput, flexible schema, simple queries by primary key. Not ideal for complex joins.

questions.question: A first Lambda invocation after a long idle period shows 800 ms of added latency. The next invocation a second later finishes in 30 ms. The 800-ms first-hit overhead is documented as the time to provision a new execution environment, download the deployment package, start the runtime, and run any module-level init. Which Lambda phenomenon is this?
options: Region cold start — one-time across all regional invocations; not the phenomenon
Billing first-invocation surcharge — not real
Cold start — execution-environment provision + runtime load + init code (typically 100 ms - 1 s)
Execution timeout — different concept; happens at the END of a too-long invocation
questions.explanation: Lambda cold start = time to provision container + load runtime + init your code. Mitigation: Provisioned Concurrency (keeps environments warm), Lambda SnapStart (Java), smaller deployment packages, faster runtimes (Node/Python vs Java).

questions.question: A network team is connecting 10 VPCs. With VPC Peering each pair needs its own peer (a full mesh = 45 peerings) AND traffic is not transitive (A→B→C does not work via two peerings). With one alternative service the team creates one hub and N spoke attachments, with transitive routing between any spokes. Which two services and which difference?
options: VPC Peering and Transit Gateway are interchangeable — false, the model is different
Transit Gateway is the legacy product; VPC Peering replaced it — false, opposite
VPC Peering = 1:1 non-transitive; Transit Gateway = hub-and-spoke with TRANSITIVE routing between attachments
VPC Peering supports more attachments than Transit Gateway — false, TGW supports many more
questions.explanation: VPC Peering: simple, low-cost, no transitive routing (A↔B and B↔C doesn't mean A↔C). Transit Gateway: scalable hub for 1000s of VPCs and VPNs with transitive routing, route tables, and multicast support.

questions.question: A compliance archive of CT scan images must be retained 30 years. Access frequency is well below 1 read per year. Retrieval latency may be 12 hours. Minimum storage cost is the only optimisation criterion. Which S3 storage class fits?
options: S3 Glacier Deep Archive — lowest per-GB cost, multi-hour retrieval, ideal for 30-yr cold archive
S3 Standard — most expensive per GB, ms retrieval, wrong for sub-yearly access
S3 Intelligent-Tiering — auto-tiers based on access; the access pattern here puts it into archive tiers ANYWAY at additional management fee
S3 One Zone-IA — single-AZ infrequent access, higher per-GB than Deep Archive
questions.explanation: S3 storage classes by access frequency: Standard > Intelligent-Tiering > Standard-IA > One Zone-IA > Glacier Instant > Glacier Flexible Retrieval > Glacier Deep Archive. Match access pattern to class to minimize costs.

questions.question: An operations engineer wants to scale capacity based on demand for: (a) EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling Group, (b) DynamoDB read/write capacity, (c) ECS service desired-count, (d) Aurora read replicas. AWS offers a unified service that orchestrates scaling across all of these. Which?
options: Scaling only available for EC2 — false; multiple services scale
AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing, doesn't perform autoscale
Elastic Load Balancing — distributes traffic, not capacity scaling
AWS Auto Scaling — orchestrates dynamic scaling across EC2 ASG, DynamoDB, ECS, Aurora replicas via target-tracking and step policies
questions.explanation: Auto Scaling policies: Target Tracking (e.g., CPU at 70%), Step Scaling (add 2 instances when CPU > 80%), Scheduled Scaling (predict load). Scaling out = add instances, Scaling in = remove instances.

questions.question: A security team wants automated, continuous scans of resource-based policies (S3 buckets, KMS keys, IAM roles, Lambda) to find resources shared EXTERNALLY (with other AWS accounts, public internet, federated principals). Findings are categorised as 'expected sharing' vs 'unintended exposure'. Which AWS service?
options: IAM Password Auditor — IAM users, not resource sharing
IAM Policy Generator wizard — authoring help, not exposure analysis
IAM Access Analyzer — continuous analysis of resource-based policies surfacing external sharing
AWS Cost Explorer — cost, unrelated
questions.explanation: IAM Access Analyzer uses automated reasoning to find S3 buckets, KMS keys, Lambda functions, IAM roles, and SQS queues that are accessible from outside your AWS account — reducing data exposure risk.

questions.question: A vendor's SaaS service runs in their AWS account. Our security team requires our VPC to consume that service over PRIVATE IPs on the AWS backbone, NOT via the public internet, without site-to-site VPN. Which service enables this private cross-account/cross-service consumption pattern?
options: AWS Client VPN — for remote user VPN, not VPC↔service private connectivity
S3 Access Points — bucket-level construct, not cross-service
AWS PrivateLink — interface endpoints in our VPC privately consume the vendor's endpoint service over AWS backbone
Direct Connect virtual interfaces — for on-prem↔AWS dedicated circuit, not in-VPC service consumption
questions.explanation: PrivateLink creates private endpoints in your VPC for AWS services (S3, DynamoDB, CloudWatch) or third-party SaaS services. Traffic stays on AWS network — no internet exposure, no NAT gateway costs for AWS service traffic.

questions.question: A finance team wants to be alerted when AWS spend hits 50%, 80%, and 100% of the monthly budget. The control must also support automatic actions (e.g., stop EC2 instances, apply an IAM policy) on threshold breach. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Bills dashboard — passive month-to-date view, no thresholds or actions
AWS Cost Explorer — historical analysis, no live thresholds
AWS Budgets — custom cost/usage budgets with email/SNS thresholds AND optional auto-actions (stop EC2, apply policy, target capacity)
AWS Compute Optimizer — recommends right-sizing, not budget alerting
questions.explanation: AWS Budgets lets you define cost/usage/RI coverage budgets with SNS email/SMS alerts. Budget Actions can automatically apply IAM policies or stop EC2/RDS instances when thresholds are crossed.

questions.question: A global service needs DNS routing that, on a per-record basis, can: route by latency to closest Region, fail over from primary to secondary on health-check fail, weight requests across blue/green deployments, geofence answers by user country, and return multiple answers with health-aware selection. Which AWS DNS service provides ALL of these routing policies?
options: Route 53 supports a single simple round-robin policy — false; many policies exist
Route 53 routing policies apply only to Alias records — false; they apply to A, AAAA, CNAME, Alias
Route 53 supports: Simple, Weighted, Latency-based, Failover, Geolocation, Geoproximity, Multivalue-Answer, IP-based
Route 53 routing is scoped to EC2 — false; targets can be any IP
questions.explanation: Route 53 routing policies enable sophisticated DNS-based traffic management: Weighted for canary deployments, Latency-based for global performance, Failover for disaster recovery, Geolocation for compliance/localization.

questions.question: Two IAM policy categories sit alongside in an account: one is AUTHORED, NUMBERED, and maintained by AWS (e.g., AmazonS3ReadOnlyAccess), the other is AUTHORED by the customer (e.g., MyAppReadOnly). The first is automatically updated when AWS adds new permissions; the second is the customer's responsibility. Which is which?
options: AWS Managed policies are pre-built, AWS-maintained, version-tracked; Customer Managed policies are customer-authored and customer-maintained
Both behave identically at evaluation time — true at IAM evaluation but they DIFFER on authorship/maintenance, which is the question
Customer Managed are inherently less secure — false
AWS Managed can only attach to users — false, they attach to users, groups, and roles
questions.explanation: AWS Managed Policies: maintained by AWS, updated automatically when services change, reusable. Customer Managed: you control content, version history, can apply fine-grained permissions. Inline policies: embedded in a single identity.

questions.question: A media site's static assets must be delivered with sub-50 ms latency to users in 50 countries. The service must cache GETs at global edge POPs, terminate TLS at the edge, and integrate with WAF + Shield. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Elemental MediaPackage — video packaging, but not the general-purpose global CDN front
AWS WAF — L7 firewall; complements CloudFront but isn't a CDN
Amazon Route 53 — DNS, not a content cache
Amazon CloudFront — global CDN with 600+ edge POPs, edge TLS termination, WAF + Shield integration
questions.explanation: CloudFront caches static and dynamic content at edge locations. Reduces origin load and latency for global users. Supports Lambda@Edge for edge compute, signed URLs/cookies for private content, and AWS WAF integration.

questions.question: An architect needs to forecast the monthly cost of a PROPOSED architecture (Lambda + DynamoDB + S3 + CloudFront + Route 53) BEFORE deploying anything. The tool must use AWS list prices and produce a per-service breakdown. Which AWS tool?
options: AWS Bills — past spend only
AWS Invoice Manager — invoicing, not forecasting
AWS Cost Saver Report — not a documented AWS product name
AWS Pricing Calculator — free web tool to estimate monthly cost for proposed architectures pre-deploy
questions.explanation: The AWS Pricing Calculator (calculator.aws.amazon.com) helps estimate costs upfront. Model EC2 instance types, storage, data transfer, and other services to build a cost estimate for budget approval or comparison.

questions.question: An organisation considers AWS Support plans. The free tier covers billing-only. Above that there are three paid tiers offering increasing response-time SLAs and channels (email vs phone vs TAM). Which describes the four tiers correctly?
options: Basic (free, billing-only), Developer (email, business-hours), Business (24×7 chat/phone, Trusted Advisor full), Enterprise (TAM, 15-min critical response)
Every plan includes 24×7 phone and a TAM — false; only Enterprise has a TAM
Every plan includes a Technical Account Manager — false; only Enterprise
Enterprise Support is free when spend crosses a threshold — false, always paid
questions.explanation: Support plan tiers: Basic (free) → Developer → Business → Enterprise On-Ramp → Enterprise. Business and above get: 24/7 phone support, full Trusted Advisor checks, and access to Infrastructure Event Management.

questions.question: An app must send 2 million transactional emails per month (purchase receipts, account-verification, password-reset) with a managed deliverability service, no SMTP server to operate. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon CloudWatch — observability, not email
Amazon GuardDuty — security threat detection, not email
Amazon SES (Simple Email Service) — managed transactional + marketing email sending at scale
Amazon WorkMail — desktop email service for business mailboxes, different use-case
questions.explanation: SES sends emails from applications (order confirmations, password resets, newsletters). Integrates with Lambda and SNS. Handles bounce/complaint processing. Can also receive emails and trigger Lambda functions.

questions.question: Security best practice in IAM says: a new IAM principal should START WITH ZERO permissions; permissions are added on a documented need-to-do basis; periodic audit removes unused permissions. Which principle is this?
options: Grant admin broadly to avoid friction — anti-pattern
Grant broad read access by default — anti-pattern
Least Privilege — minimum permissions; start with none, add as required, audit + prune regularly
Apply to users only, exempt roles — false, applies equally to roles
questions.explanation: Least privilege: users, roles, and services should have only the exact permissions they need. Use IAM Access Advisor to see last used permissions. Remove unused permissions. Prefer managed policies over wildcard (*) actions.

questions.question: A team needs MANAGED file systems for specific protocols: SMB for Windows file shares, Lustre for high-performance computing, NetApp ONTAP for migration from on-prem ONTAP, OpenZFS for ZFS workloads. They want one AWS service family that covers all four. Which?
options: A new EBS volume type — block storage, not file-system
Amazon FSx (FSx for Windows / Lustre / NetApp ONTAP / OpenZFS) — managed file-system family covering each protocol/engine
Amazon EFS — NFS only; doesn't cover SMB/Lustre/ONTAP/ZFS
AWS Storage Gateway — exposes S3 as on-prem file shares; different surface than FSx
questions.explanation: FSx is the managed file-systems family: Windows File Server (SMB), Lustre (HPC), NetApp ONTAP, OpenZFS. Storage Gateway is different (hybrid). PRIOR VERSION HAD WRONG CORRECT-ANSWER INDEX (marked Storage Gateway as the FSx definition) — fixed 2026-05-13.

questions.question: An on-prem NAS holds 200 TB of files that must be migrated INCREMENTALLY (initial bulk + ongoing deltas) to Amazon S3 and EFS. The team wants a managed service with bandwidth throttling, encryption in transit, scheduling, and integrity verification — without writing custom scripts. Which service?
options: AWS DMS — database migration, not file/NAS
RDS read-replica — DB replication, unrelated
DynamoDB Global Tables — multi-region DDB, unrelated
AWS DataSync — managed online file/object data-transfer accelerator with scheduling, throttling, and integrity verification
questions.explanation: DataSync automates and accelerates data migration/sync. Uses a DataSync Agent on-premises. Handles scheduling, monitoring, encryption, and data validation. Ideal for one-time migrations or ongoing data processing workflows.

questions.question: Under the Shared Responsibility Model, for a Lambda function deployed in customer code, who is responsible for: (a) hypervisor patching, (b) Lambda runtime (e.g., python3.12) patching, (c) the customer's function CODE, (d) the IAM role attached, (e) the data the function reads/writes?
options: Customer owns the runtime + OS — false, AWS owns the Lambda runtime + OS
Customer handles OS patching only — false, AWS handles OS + runtime
Identical split to EC2 — false, Lambda is more managed than EC2
AWS handles infrastructure + OS + runtime patching; customer handles function code, IAM role, data, and config
questions.explanation: Serverless shifts more responsibility to AWS. For Lambda, you don't manage: servers, OS, runtime patches, capacity. You still own: your code, IAM roles, data encryption, network access, and application-level security.

questions.question: A web/mobile app needs a managed identity service for END USERS (not AWS administrators). Requirements: user sign-up / sign-in with email or social login (Google, Facebook), MFA, password-reset, and a federated path to obtain AWS credentials for direct service calls. Which AWS service?
options: Amazon RDS — relational database, not an identity service
AWS IAM — for AWS administrators / workloads, not end users of an app
Amazon Cognito — User Pools (directory + sign-up/in) + Identity Pools (federated AWS credentials)
AWS Client VPN — network VPN auth, unrelated
questions.explanation: Cognito User Pools: user directory, handles sign-up/sign-in, MFA, OAuth2. Identity Pools (Federated Identities): swap tokens from social providers (Google, Facebook) or User Pools for temporary AWS credentials.

questions.question: A company has Oracle, SQL Server, and Windows Server licences they own (BYOL). They want a managed inventory tool that tracks each license, attaches them to AWS / on-prem instances, and alerts when a deployment would exceed the licence count. Which AWS service?
options: AWS License Manager — manage BYOL licences across AWS + on-prem, enforce limits, generate reports
AWS Marketplace — buy 3rd-party software, not manage BYOL
AWS Cost Explorer — cost analytics, not licence inventory
AWS Resource Groups — group resources, not licence tracking
questions.explanation: License Manager helps track BYOL (Bring Your Own License) software deployments on EC2, prevents launching instances that would violate license terms, and provides a centralized dashboard for license inventory.

questions.question: A workload in a single AZ is taken offline when that AZ has a utility-power incident. The architect spreads the workload across 3 AZs in the same Region. Why does this design eliminate the single-AZ failure?
options: AZs are labels for the same DC, no real isolation — false
AZs share power and cooling — false
AZs are physically separate facilities with independent power, cooling, and network; multi-AZ design survives single-AZ failure
Multi-AZ doubles cost regardless of architecture — generic false; cost varies by service
questions.explanation: Each AZ is one or more discrete data centers with redundant power/network. They're connected with low-latency links but isolated from each other's failures. Multi-AZ = high availability. ELB + Auto Scaling + RDS Multi-AZ = HA architecture.

questions.question: An enterprise wants AWS to set up a multi-account 'landing zone' for them — pre-baked OUs, guardrails enforced via SCPs, a 'log archive' account, an 'audit' account, an Account Factory for new accounts. They want this in a few clicks, not via custom CloudFormation. Which AWS service?
options: AWS Data Center Inventory — not a real service
AWS Artifact — compliance docs, unrelated
AWS IAM role lifecycle manager — not a real service
AWS Control Tower — automates a multi-account Landing Zone (OUs, SCP guardrails, log/audit accounts, Account Factory)
questions.explanation: Control Tower builds a Landing Zone with: Log Archive account, Audit account, and an Account Factory. Guardrails (preventive = SCPs, detective = Config Rules) enforce compliance automatically across all accounts.

questions.question: Finance asks BI for monthly KPI dashboards over Athena/Redshift/RDS data, accessible in a browser, no servers to operate, with per-reader pricing. Which AWS service fits?
options: CloudWatch — operational metrics dashboards, NOT a BI tool over warehouses
Amazon QuickSight — serverless BI: dashboards over S3 / Redshift / Athena / RDS / databases, per-reader pricing
AWS Glue — ETL service, doesn't render BI dashboards
AWS CloudTrail — control-plane audit logs, not BI
questions.explanation: QuickSight connects to dozens of data sources and enables self-service BI with SPICE (in-memory computation engine). ML Insights adds anomaly detection and forecasting. Pay-per-session pricing model.

questions.question: A finance team compares EC2 cost models: (a) ~12 months of free usage on small instance types, (b) per-hour pay-as-you-go, (c) 1- or 3-year commitment with 40-72% discount, (d) interruptible spare capacity at up to 90% off. Which mapping is correct?
options: All four have the same effective hourly rate — false
Spot is dedicated long-running capacity — false, it is INTERRUPTIBLE
Reserved is more expensive than On-Demand — false, opposite
Free Tier = 12-month free for limited usage; On-Demand = pay-as-you-go; Reserved = 1/3-yr commit with big discount; Spot = interruptible spare capacity at deep discount
questions.explanation: EC2 pricing: On-Demand (full price, flexible), RI Standard (fixed type, ~72% off, 1-3yr), RI Convertible (~66% off, can change type), Spot (bid on spare capacity, cheapest, interruptible with 2-min notice), Savings Plans (flexible commitment).
